scope: A verified annotated bibliography for the force fleet: SIPRI's 2024 military-expenditure and arms-transfer fact sheets; MP-IDSA and ORF defence-budget and procurement analyses by Laxman Kumar Behera; PRS Demand for Grants analyses for Defence and Home Affairs 2025-26 and PRS's 2017 police-reform report; the Common Cause–CSDS Status of Policing in India reports (2018, 2019, 2023, 2025); the Prakash Singh judgment; the Standing Committee reports as transcribed by PRS; the Agnipath debate papers on both sides; the CAG single-vendor finding; the comparative police-strength literature; and the court records and journalism of record for Bofors, Rafale, AgustaWestland, Tatra, Adarsh and Pegasus. Each document carries a two-sentence summary of what it establishes and what it does not. The file calibrates fifteen narratives the other seven domains will rate and sets base rates (police per lakh against the unverified 222 benchmark; defence share of GDP against the SIPRI peer set; pension share; CAPF vacancy; single-vendor share). It leaves out: the budget series themselves (union-defence, union-home and state-police domains write those rows; this file carries no series rows to avoid key collisions), footprint, procurement awards, and any claim about a person. Reachability: bprd.nic.in and cag.gov.in were unreachable (connection failed); pib.gov.in, factly.in, Wiley, Taylor & Francis and MIT Press returned 403 to the fetcher; Takshashila and CPR searches returned no police-reform results; CHRI's compliance page and the Sukna Wikipedia page returned 404. Wikipedia pages were used as summaries of court and press records for the cases (tier reported) where the primary order was not opened.

entities.label: Prakash Singh & Ors v Union of India (SC, 2006-09-22)
entities.sub: Supreme Court judgment (Sabharwal CJI, Thakker J, Balasubramanyan J) issuing seven binding directives on police organisation to the Union and the states
entities.publicRole: Published analysis, audit, judgment or survey that other domains in this fleet cite; recorded for what it establishes and what it does not.
d: Establishes: seven directives — a State Security Commission; DGP selection from a UPSC-empanelled list of three senior-most officers with a minimum two-year tenure; two-year minimum tenure for IG, DIG, SP and SHO; separation of investigation from law and order (first in towns above 10 lakh); a Police Establishment Board for transfers below DSP; Police Complaints Authorities at state (retired HC/SC judge) and district (retired district judge) level; a National Security Commission to select CAPF chiefs with two-year tenure [documented]

entities.label: ORF — The Case for Agnipath (Behera & Kaushal, 2023)
entities.sub: ORF Issue Brief No. 567, 16 August 2023 (updated from 2022), Laxman Kumar Behera and Vinay Kaushal — the proponents' economic case
entities.publicRole: Published analysis, audit, judgment or survey that other domains in this fleet cite; recorded for what it establishes and what it does not.
d: Establishes: defence pension rose 163% from ₹45,500 crore (2013-14) to ₹1,19,696 crore (2022-23) while total MoD spending rose 107%; pay & allowances plus pension ₹2,87,040 crore = 79% of revenue expenditure in 2022-23; military pensioners 3.8 lakh (1950), 6 lakh (1970), 26.8 lakh (2021); an Agniveer's composite pay ₹30,000 (year 1) to ₹40,000 (year 4) a month, ₹45,338 average including the government's 30% Seva Nidhi contribution, against ₹59,976 for a regular soldier — ₹1,75,656 less a year; first-year saving ₹1,054 crore on 60,000 recruits; the authors state "there will be no savings in the near to medium term" and pension savings arrive only after 2044, when 34% (4,54,688 of 13.3 lakh other ranks) would be pensionable; MoD projects average age falling from 32 to 24–26 [reported]

Does not establish: operational effects — the brief concedes teething problems, infrastructure costs for larger training cohorts, and that the officer cadre is "equally ripe for reform"; it is an argument for the scheme, written by its best-known defender [analytic]

narratives.claim: Rafale was a scam: the price was inflated and Reliance was favoured as offset partner at the government's behest.
narratives.strongestCase: A 36-aircraft purchase replaced a 126-aircraft tender in April 2015; Reliance Defence was incorporated days before; the former French President said the Indian side proposed Reliance; opposition figures put the per-aircraft price at ₹1,570 crore against ₹526 crore; a French judicial investigation has been open since June 2021 and France complained in 2023 of Indian delays on cooperation.
narratives.strongestCounter: The Supreme Court (2018-12-14; review 2019-11-14) found the process broadly followed, declined to compare prices, and held offset-partner choice rests with the vendor under the Offset Guidelines; Dassault and the French ministry said the choice was theirs; the government's like-for-like price comparison (9–20% saving) was never contradicted by a court or audit opened here; Reliance's share of the offsets was stated at ₹6,500 crore of ₹30,000 crore; no court or audit has found corruption.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up: a finding by the French investigating judge of payments to Indian decision-makers, or the CAG report (unopened) showing the IGA dearer than the escalated bid. Down to debunked: the French probe closes with no finding.
srcs: Indian Kanoon — Manohar Lal Sharma v Narendra Damodardas Modi, SC, 2018-12-14

narratives.claim: The Prime Minister's Office ran parallel negotiations on Rafale over the Defence Ministry's objection.

narratives.strongestCounter: The Court nonetheless dismissed the review (2019-11-14); the government said the final deal was approved through the full DAC/CCS chain and that the Defence Minister of the day overruled the objection; an internal dissent note is evidence of debate, not of wrongdoing.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Down: publication of the full file showing the objection was answered on the record. Up to established: the complete MoD file in the public domain.

narratives.claim: Bofors was buried: the Congress governments protected the recipients of the kickbacks.
narratives.strongestCase: Agent payments are documented in Swiss accounts; the newspaper that broke the story stopped publishing under government pressure (per Wikipedia); the Italian agent was allowed to leave India in 1993 and extradition failed twice; CBI sought closure in 2011; the case ended in 2026 without any conviction after 39 years.
narratives.strongestCounter: Delhi HC (2004) found after 13 years of CBI investigation no evidence that any public servant received a bribe and held the late Prime Minister entitled to be seen as innocent; the Swedish investigator who leaked the documents said in 2012 there was no evidence of payment to him; the Hindujas were discharged in 2005; non-Congress governments (1989–91, 1998–2004) held the file too and did not convict anyone.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up: a recipient-side bank record naming an Indian public servant. Down: the 2026 SC order's reasons, if they find the CBI's revival meritless on evidence rather than delay.

narratives.claim: The Indian government used Pegasus on opposition politicians, journalists and judges.
narratives.strongestCase: About 300 Indian numbers on the leaked NSO client-interest list; Amnesty forensics found infections on some Indian phones; the Union refused to tell the Supreme Court whether it bought Pegasus; the SC committee found malware on 5 of 29 devices and recorded that the government did not cooperate; NSO sells only to governments.
narratives.strongestCounter: The committee could not establish that the malware was Pegasus or who deployed it; the IT Minister said the reports had no factual basis; a number on a list is not an infection; the committee report is sealed and the sample is 29 phones.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up: unsealing of the committee report with attribution, or a contract record for an Indian agency. Down: a forensic attribution of the five infections to a non-state or foreign actor.

narratives.claim: AgustaWestland bribes reached the top of the UPA government and the Air Force.
narratives.strongestCase: A middleman's note allocates about €30 million across "AF", "BUR", "Pol" and others; the altitude requirement was lowered before the tender; Italy arrested the supplier's CEO; India cancelled the contract for integrity-pact breach and recovered ₹2,068 crore; CBI arrested the former IAF chief and extradited the middleman.
narratives.strongestCounter: The Italian courts acquitted everyone on corruption at final instance (2018, upheld 2019); the Busto Arsizio court acquitted the former IAF chief in 2014; the Indian trial is pending after twelve years with no verdict; the Supreme Court granted the middleman bail in 2025.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up: a conviction in the Delhi CBI court. Down: acquittal or discharge of the Indian accused.

narratives.claim: India under-spends on defence; it should spend 3% of GDP.
narratives.strongestCase: The Standing Committee on Defence (2018) recommended about 3%; PRS puts 2025-26 at 1.9% of GDP, 13% of Union expenditure against 17% in 2014-15; capital outlay stays below 30%; the Ministry reports committed-liability shortfalls and received ₹9.01 lakh crore for 2021-26 against a higher projection.
narratives.strongestCounter: SIPRI puts India fifth in the world at US$86.1 billion, 2.3% of GDP — exactly the median of the fifteen largest spenders and near the 2.5% world average; the 3% target has no peer basis; the services' projections are demands.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: This is a value question about the denominator. It moves only if a capability audit (CAG) ties a shortfall to a documented operational gap.

narratives.claim: Agnipath is a cost-cutting measure disguised as military reform.

narratives.claim: India is dangerously under-policed: the UN recommends 222 police per lakh and India has 155.
narratives.strongestCase: BPR&D (via PRS) gives 155 per lakh on 2023-01-01, Bihar 81; the states fill only about 77% of sanctioned posts (SPIR 2019); PRS 2017 and the Standing Committee repeat the 222 norm.

narratives.claim: Custodial torture is routine and the police themselves justify it.
narratives.strongestCase: SPIR 2025: about one in ten police personnel justify third-degree methods, 11% find hitting an absconding accused's family absolutely justified, 30% would bar lawyers from interrogation; SPIR 2018: half of citizens condone custodial violence against criminals; NCRB counting gaps documented in SPIR 2025 chapter 8.
narratives.strongestCounter: These are self-reported attitudes over samples, not incidence; the majority in every item do not justify torture; official custodial-death counts are low (and contested as undercounts); India has not ratified the Convention Against Torture, so no treaty-body data exist.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: State-wise custodial deaths per lakh officers (NCRB, Parliament answers) joined by the state-police domain would turn an attitude rate into an outcome rate.

narratives.claim: Defence procurement is rigged through single-vendor tenders.
narratives.strongestCase: CAG Report No. 4 of 2007 found 60% of audited cases ended with a single vendor qualified; DAP 2020 still provides for ab-initio single-vendor and IGA/FMS routes without offsets; the fleet's CPPP slice shows services' headquarters buying with 40%+ single bids.
narratives.strongestCounter: The CAG attributed single-vendor outcomes to badly drafted qualitative requirements, not favour; much defence equipment has one or two makers worldwide; the works branch (79% of the security slice) single-bids at 0.1%; "rigged" requires a beneficiary and a mechanism that no audit opened here names.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Up: a later CAG compendium (unopened; cag.gov.in blocked) tying single-vendor cases to specific vendors and officials. Down: a current single-vendor rate near commercial norms.

narratives.claim: India is the world's largest arms importer, proving Make in India has failed.
narratives.strongestCase: SIPRI ranks India second (behind wartime Ukraine) with 8.3% of global imports 2020–24; SIPRI notes continued reliance on imports for combat aircraft.

narratives.claim: Adarsh: the Army brass and politicians stole flats meant for Kargil widows.
narratives.strongestCase: A state judicial commission (2013) indicted four former Chief Ministers, two ministers and 12 bureaucrats and found 25 illegal allotments including 22 benami; CBI arrested two retired Major Generals and others in 2012; Bombay HC ordered demolition in 2016.
narratives.strongestCounter: The state government rejected the commission report; no conviction in fourteen years; the HC quashed the sanction to prosecute a former CM (2017); the SC stayed demolition (2018); the land's ownership (state vs defence) was itself disputed.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A CBI court verdict either way.

narratives.claim: Tatra: the Army bought 7,000 overpriced trucks for 25 years through a middleman protected by BEML.
narratives.strongestCase: The then Army chief said in 2012 he was offered ₹14 crore to clear a tranche; about 7,000 trucks were bought over two decades through a single public-sector channel.
narratives.strongestCounter: Nothing opened in this sweep records the CBI outcome, BEML's stated case or any pricing audit; a bribe offer alleged by the buyer's own chief is evidence the offer was refused, not that prior purchases were corrupt.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Opening the CBI closure report or chargesheet and the Defence Minister's statement to Parliament (2012) would move this to contested or unsupported.

symmetryCheck: Cases: Bofors (Congress era) beside Rafale (BJP era) with identical fields — document trail (Swedish Radio/The Hindu 1987; The Hindu 2019), court record (Delhi HC 2004: no evidence any public servant received a bribe; SC 2018: no reason to intervene, review dismissed 2019), audit (JPC 1988 not opened; CAG 2019 not opened), foreign probe (Swiss documents 1997; French PNF 2021–), outcome (no conviction in either). The lens produces the same shape for both governments: documented process anomalies, documented agent-side or dissent-side paper, and a judiciary that declined to find corruption. AgustaWestland beside Tatra (both UPA-era, both CBI cases from 2012–13): the record is dense for one and a stub for the other, which is a finding about attention, not guilt. Literature: the principal budget analyst (Behera) wrote the IDSA series under both UPA and NDA and the ORF Agnipath brief under NDA; his adequacy measure (projection-vs-allocation gap) was 27% in UPA's last year and 25–30% in 2018–20, so the method does not flatter either side. The SPIR attitude series exists only for 2018–25, so no UPA baseline can be run; this is recorded as a void rather than inferred. States: this domain holds no state rows; the SPIR tables (reserved-post vacancies highest in UP and Haryana; premature transfers highest in Haryana and UP, both BJP-run in 2016; constabulary ratio met only in West Bengal and Bihar, opposition-run) are reported as printed and party is text only.
